opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the two are very closely intertwined, but they're not quite the same thing. Formal logic is really the foundation: it gives you the rules of the game. It tells you what a valid inference is, how you're allowed to derive one statement from another, and what the basic syntax of your statements looks like. Whether you're working in first-order logic, higher-order logic, or some kind of dependent type theory, the logic is what defines what counts as a correct step.

Formal mathematics, on the other hand, is about actually building mathematics on top of that foundation. You take a logical framework, say set theory on top of first-order logic, or type theory as in systems like Lean or Coq, or higher-order logic as in HOL Light or Isabelle, and then you start formalizing definitions, theorems, and proofs: the real numbers, analysis, algebra, topology, all the way up to serious research-level results. Every step is checked mechanically by a computer against the rules of the underlying logic.

So the way I like to think about it, formal logic is a bit like the instruction set of a processor, and formal mathematics is like the large software ecosystem built on top of it. In principle everything reduces to those primitive steps, but in practice the interesting part, and the hard part, is the enormous amount of structure, libraries, definitions, and abstractions you need so that mathematicians can work at a reasonable level without thinking about the low-level details.

That's also why I find this area so interesting from an AI perspective. The logic gives you a perfectly reliable verifier: you always know whether a proof is correct. But formal mathematics is where the real challenge lies, because the search space is huge, and translating the way human mathematicians actually reason, which is very informal and intuitive, into this rigorous, fully formal setting is extremely labor-intensive. My hope has long been that we can build systems that bridge that gap: that read informal mathematics, autoformalize it, and eventually reason at a level where they can contribute new mathematics, with the formal logic acting as the ground truth that keeps everything honest.

r001.rationale: The response says formal mathematics is built on logical foundations and describes it as a software ecosystem, but does not clearly characterize formal mathematics as logic made executable as a computer program.

r002.rationale: It says computers mechanically check each step and calls logic a reliable verifier, but does not state that proofs have so many individual steps that manual checking is impractical.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I see it, formal mathematics is basically mathematics done inside a formal logic. So the logic is the framework, and the mathematics is what you build inside that framework. If you look at something like Lean or Coq or Isabelle, each of these has a particular logical foundation underneath it. Isabelle/HOL is based on higher-order logic, Lean and Coq are based on variants of dependent type theory, and Metamath is set-theoretic, basically ZFC written out very explicitly. And then on top of that logical core, you formalize definitions, you state theorems, and you construct proofs that the kernel can check mechanically.

So the relationship is really one of foundation and superstructure. The logic gives you the rules of the game, what counts as a valid inference step, and the mathematics is the actual content, the actual structures you care about, groups, topological spaces, real numbers, whatever it is. And what's interesting is that for most working mathematicians, the particular choice of logic doesn't matter that much. They work informally, and they have an implicit trust that whatever they do could in principle be reduced to some foundation. Formal mathematics is where you actually make that reduction explicit and let a computer verify it.

From the machine learning side, this is what makes it so attractive to me. Because once everything is formal, you have a completely unambiguous notion of correctness. A proof either checks or it doesn't. There's no human judgment involved in verifying the result, which means you get a perfect reward signal for training systems. And at the same time, the mathematics layer is where all the interesting creativity happens, the choice of what to define, which lemmas to prove, how to structure an argument. So the logic gives you the rigor, and the mathematics gives you the richness, and the combination is really what makes formal reasoning a great testbed for AI.

r001.rationale: The response says formal mathematics is built inside formal logic and that a kernel checks proofs, but does not characterize it as logic made executable as a computer program.

r002.rationale: The response says computers can check proofs mechanically, but does not state that proofs contain so many steps that manual checking is impractical.

astra-6.text:
I think of formal logic as the foundation—the language and the rules of inference—and formal mathematics as what you build on top of that. You specify your axioms and definitions, and a proof shows how a statement follows from them according to those rules.

But doing mathematics is very different from simply applying rules. You have to find useful definitions, recognize patterns, and decide which intermediate statements will help you. The logical foundation tells you whether a step is valid; it doesn’t tell you which step is worth taking.

That distinction is particularly interesting for AI. You can have a system that searches for proofs in a very creative, heuristic way, while a formal proof checker verifies the result. So the process of discovering mathematics can be uncertain, even though checking the resulting proof is precise.

r001.rationale: The response describes logic as the foundation and formal mathematics as built on it, but does not characterize formal mathematics as logic made executable as a computer program.

r002.rationale: It says a formal proof checker can verify a result, but does not state that computers can feasibly check proofs with many steps that would be impractical to check manually.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of formal logic as providing the language and the rules of inference, while formal mathematics is what you build using those rules. You specify your axioms and definitions, and a proof tells you, step by step, how a statement follows from them.

In everyday mathematics, we leave a lot of those steps implicit. We rely on intuition and on the reader understanding what we mean. Formalization makes those dependencies explicit enough that a computer can check them. That doesn’t remove the creative part of mathematics—finding the right definitions, conjectures, and arguments. It gives you a precise way to verify the result of that creative process.

r001.rationale: The response describes formal mathematics as built using logic’s language and inference rules, and says computers can check formalizations. It does not characterize formal mathematics as logic made executable as a computer program.

r002.rationale: The response says explicit dependencies let a computer check a proof, but does not state that proofs have so many steps that manual checking is impractical.
